course.title: Policy Evaluation Lab
course.details: Master's degree (LM) · ECON-02/A · 60 hours · 9 CFU · first semester · taught in English
course.office_hours: By appointment via e-mail (day and time to be confirmed)
course.timetable: Monday, Thursday and Friday, 5:00–7:00 pm · Room 20, Department of Business Economics (Economia Aziendale)

announcements.title: Welcome to the Policy Evaluation Lab
announcements.body: Slides, datasets, exercises and exam information are posted here. Slides go up before each lecture; datasets and exercises after it. Bring a laptop to the lab sessions.

weeks.summary: Descriptive analysis versus causal inference; potential outcomes, the counterfactual and selection bias. Software set-up.
OLS as a comparison of means, control variables, omitted-variable bias; robust and clustered standard errors.
Why randomisation solves selection bias; balance checks, compliance, intention-to-treat. Case study: Tennessee STAR.
Conditional independence, matching, the propensity score and inverse probability weighting.
The 2×2 design, parallel trends, regression formulation. Lab: Card and Krueger (1994) on the New Jersey minimum wage.
Event studies and pre-trends; staggered adoption and the problems of two-way fixed effects.
Relevance and exclusion, 2SLS, weak instruments, LATE. Lab: Angrist and Krueger (1991) on compulsory schooling.
Sharp and fuzzy designs, bandwidth choice, manipulation tests.
Building a counterfactual from a donor pool; inference by placebo. Case study: California Proposition 99.

exercises.title: Interactive practice on EconVis
exercises.description: Guided challenges, detective mode and interpretation quizzes, with the simulated data downloadable as CSV to rerun in R or Excel.

exercises.title: Problem sets
exercises.description: One problem set per method, posted after the corresponding lab. Solutions are released one week later.

exam.intro: A report on a policy intervention of your choice, presented in the last week of the course, followed by an oral exam.

parts.title: Report
parts.description: On a policy intervention of your choice: either an empirical analysis in R with real-world data, or an argument based on explanation and evidence. The policy can be one you assess as successful or unsuccessful; either way, you have to argue your thesis properly, using solid evidence.

parts.title: Presentation
parts.description: You present your report in the last week of the course (week 10).

parts.title: Oral exam
parts.description: Written instead, if the number of students does not allow us to complete the orals on time.
